comments, in respect of previous matters were as

issued formal rejection of AEH as supplier.  In my

AEH's compliance statement was never challenged on

vision clarity" and a sample panel for "workmanship and
quality" were requested, but not brightness, which is
not the same as image clarity; as brightness increases,
image clarity can be lost by glare.  And this was never
formally instructed, and neither were the size, location
and purpose ever defined.
Next, please.
Turning to the levels of approval.  In the
Construction and Projects Department's policy and
procedure, the document that defined the parameters for
submittals and approvals for the process of the project
were as follows.
"APP" was "approved": the drawing was approved as
it was submitted and work can proceed.
Critically, "AAN", "approved as noted", the drawing
is approved with comments written on the drawings.  The
drawing needs to be revised and resubmitted for APP
status; but, critically, work can proceed as long as
the comments are incorporated.
The third criteria is "ANR": "approved as noted,
resubmit".  The drawing is approved with comments in
writing on the drawing, but the drawing needs to be
revised and resubmitted for APP status, and no work can
proceed on the basis of the drawing as it stands at that
particular point in time.
Finally, there's "not approved".  The drawing is
rejected, usually for reasons stated thereon, and must
be resubmitted and no work can proceed.
In my experience, although sometimes called
different things, such as "Status A, B, C and D", having
four levels of approval on similar terms to the above is
typical in probably all 50 other projects I've been
involved with in dealing with these submittals.  It is
a typical feature of the review and approvals procedure
in most construction contracts.
The respondent's position would seem to be that
"AAN" is not approval.  In my experience, this is
clearly not the case.  "AAN" means that work can proceed
so long as changes are incorporated that address
the comments that have been made.
In my opinion, repeated AAN status responses,
without rejection, reasonably permits procurement and
progression, as per the DIEZA manual.  Moreover,
elements of the submission that are not the subject of
any comments, these are approved, as the AAN description
makes clear that "work can proceed so long as
the comments are incorporated".

only statement made in the media screen specification

might be too bright and produce glare, or that
8,000 nits might still not be bright enough.
It may also be an acceptance that image clarity
might not always be a factor of brightness, but would be
influenced by the type and relative placement of the

the face of the inner pane of the double-glazed units,

acceptance criteria methodology, viewing conditions or
benchmark environmental conditions, it is not clear how
the mockup was to be assessed.
Next, please.
In terms of approval "Subject to client acceptance",

does not envisage the client being involved in the
acceptance procedure.  I am persuaded this is the case
by clause 3.3 of the contract, which stated:
"The Contractor shall only take instructions from
the Engineer ..."
And also:
"The Contractor shall comply with the instructions
given by the Engineer ... on any matter related to
the Contract."
Even if the client had a right to accept or reject
work, the acceptance or rejection of any submission or
item of work would have to be made in accordance with
the contract.
Rejection of a mockup, for example, could only be
made if the mockup failed the predefined mockup
requirements.  As there was no defined testing protocol,
acceptance criteria methodology, viewing conditions or
benchmark environmental conditions, it is not clear what
ground could legitimately be cited for its rejection.
Next, please.
Coming to conflicts in the specification.
The media screens specification attempted to achieve
mutually competing objectives.  The specification
required a high transparency; it also required a high
brightness level.  The two requirements were in direct
conflict, as increasing the number of LEDs to increase
brightness reduced the transparency level and increased
the heat levels.
Although I have seen no evidence that the brightness

properly measured, it would seem to be accepted that
AEH's screens achieved the transparency but not the
brightness, whereas Mediaglass's screens achieved
the brightness at the expense of the transparency
requirements.
There were also other interrelated specification
terms and competing criteria.  The size of the screen
and the type of media that was displayed, the pixel
spacing and the optimum viewing distance are all
interrelated factors.
For example, the smallest screen, which is just over
5m by about 7.5m, if it was supposed to show a video,
a pixel pitch of 25mm would be required and the optimum
viewing distance would be 25.6m away.  Given the
locations of the two smallest screens on B1 and B6,
I would suggest that their viewing distance was somewhat
greater than that, so this is rather an anomaly; if they
were to display videos, that was.
Next, please.
In terms of normal industrial practice, in my
experience, it would be normal practice for the engineer
to ascertain from its client what the purpose of each
screen was, be that videos, cartoons, static adverts or
atmospheric illumination, et cetera.
Given the layouts of the buildings, the designer
would agree with the client where the screens would be
and where they would be viewed from, ie the centre of
the plaza or a caf on the opposite site, for example.
From this information, the designer would then work out
the optimum size of the screen based upon pixel pitches

transparency.
These criteria would be stated on a screen-by-screen

the contractor can define without guidance from
the engineer in the specification.
If a mockup is required, its size, purpose and the
criteria upon which acceptance will be achieved needs to
be stated, ie nits levels to be achieved and by what
colours, viewing and environmental conditions for
the tests or benchmark conditions, along with the
methodology whereby the parameters which govern
acceptance of each criteria will be measured.
It's industry practice to reject a submission,
whether at PQ, MAR or technical submission status, if
the proposed system is fundamentally unacceptable.
It would be industry practice to instruct a redesign if
the proposed system could work feasibly, but required
considerable work to achieve the specified outcome.
It would be industry practice to define/instruct revised
criteria for the system if the client's objectives
change or if it becomes clear that there is an error or
conflict with the previously specified criteria.
There should be no need to prohibit procurement, as
the approval status the engineer gives a submission
normally governs whether the approval allows
the contractor to proceed or not.

competing technical requirements, including transparency

acceptance benchmark was identified.  Requests were made
regarding image clarity, quality of product and
workmanship, but no measured brightness criteria.
The engineer continued reviewing AEH submissions

reduced the overall size of the screen without
instructing a commensurate reduction in pixel pitch in
order to maintain the picture quality.
In my opinion, responsibility for unresolved
performance criteria remained with the engineer and
the design team.
